meanings.note: Reflexive verb; familiar imperative siediti attaches ti onto the end.

examples.trans: We sit down at the table.

meanings.note: Ownership, age (avere venti anni), and idioms like avere voglia di.
Forms compound past tenses of transitive verbs.
Irregular future vedrete ('you all will see') and past participle visto ('seen / watched').

examples.trans: Do you see those light stands?

meanings.note: Feminine plural definite article (le cose, le puntate).
Indirect object 'to her' or feminine plural direct object.
Ordinal adjective; on a film slate, feminines prima / seconda stand for prima ripresa ('first take').

examples.text: Ho visto le prime due puntate.
examples.trans: I watched the first two episodes.

meanings.note: Invariable cardinal number.
Standard Italian word for an episode of a television series or programme.
Written with an accent to distinguish it from reflexive/impersonal pronoun si.

examples.trans: Yes, I am coming right away.

meanings.note: Indefinite pronoun for an unspecified thing or small amount.

examples.trans: Do you want something to drink?
I watched a little bit yesterday.

meanings.note: Unstressed familiar 2nd-person singular direct, indirect, or reflexive pronoun.
Identity, description, location, and passive/intransitive auxiliary; with ci forms c'è ('there is').
The thing liked is the grammatical subject (ti piace Seppia?, ti è piaciuta la fotografia?).
Feminine singular definite article (la scena, la regia).
Third-person feminine singular direct object clitic (non la dico, la risolviamo).
In film and TV, refers to the lighting and camera look created by the director of photography.

examples.text: La fotografia del film è bellissima.

meanings.note: Invariable adverb modifying a verb or answering a question on its own.
Standard negative particle placed immediately before the verb (plus any clitics).
Takes -isc- in singular and 3rd plural present forms; capito? checks understanding.
Negative pronoun; pairs with non before the verb (non vuoi niente, non fa niente).
Core verb used in many idioms: non fa niente, fare schifo, farsi la doccia, fare il bravo.
Fare schifo ('to make disgust') is the everyday idiom for 'to suck / be awful'.
Masculine singular definite article before s + consonant, z, gn, ps.
Unstressed 3rd-person masculine/neuter direct object pronoun before a verb (non lo so).

sapere.gloss: to know (a fact or how to)

meanings.note: Knowing facts or answers (sa dov'è?, non lo so).
Followed directly by an infinitive (sai giocare?, 'do you know how to play?').

examples.trans: Do you know how to play foosball?

meanings.note: Single Italian word covering both question 'why?' and answer 'because'.

examples.trans: I am laughing because it is funny.

meanings.note: Expresses desire or intention; imperfect volevo softens a polite request.
Third-person plural pronoun; placed after the verb for strong contrast (lo vogliono loro).

examples.trans: They are the ones deciding it.

meanings.note: Modal verb followed directly by an infinitive.

examples.trans: I have to talk to you.

meanings.note: Forms comparatives before adjectives (più bella, 'prettier').

examples.trans: I am not speaking any more.

meanings.note: Before nouns, masculine singular adapts like the article: bel, bell', bello.

examples.trans: It is a very fine film.

meanings.note: Contraction of di + feminine singular article la; after più, introduces comparison.
Invariable feminine noun ending in a stressed vowel.
Introduces a condition (se vuoi, se ti va, se no 'otherwise').

examples.text: Se ti va, prendiamo un caffè.
examples.trans: If you fancy it, let us get a coffee.

meanings.note: Negative reply; in se no ('if not'), means 'otherwise'.

examples.trans: Run, otherwise you will be late.

meanings.note: Grammatically singular feminine collective noun in Italian: la gente cambia.
Used both transitively (cambiare canale) and intransitively (le cose cambiano).
Broadcast station; also a water canal.

examples.text: Su che canale è il film?
examples.trans: What channel is the film on?

meanings.note: Takes a before a noun/pronoun ('think about/of': pensare a tutto) and di before an infinitive.

examples.trans: I am thinking of coming back tomorrow.

meanings.note: Marks destination, location in cities, or indirect recipient.
Links activities and idioms such as giocare a tennis or a presto.
Singular tutto alone means 'everything'; masculine plural tutti alone means 'everyone'.
Marks beneficiary (per i ragazzi), duration/target (quanto per Corinna?), or reason (scusa per prima).
Dramatic unit of a script or film.

examples.trans: In the scene she is asleep.

meanings.note: With via, mandare via means sending someone away or kicking them out.

examples.trans: I will send you a message.

meanings.note: Used with verbs of motion or sending (mandare via, 'send away').
Shortens to buon before most masculine nouns; on set, Buona! approves a take.
Used in wishes such as Buona serata! ('Have a nice evening!').
